units.text: This circular summarises the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) recent observations of licensed corporations’ practices in offering and promoting SFC-authorised funds. Intermediaries who distribute these funds (distributors) have been offering additional returns or other incentives that may divert the client’s focus from properly considering the risks and features of the underlying funds. This circular also highlights the legal and regulatory requirements to be met by distributors.
Background

In some cases, distributors promoted SFC-authorised funds (often via online platforms) and offered or imposed additional or distinct features or restrictions (eg, “guaranteed returns” or “lock-up periods”) beyond the product features set out in the funds’ offering documents.

In other cases, distributors asked clients to provide a mandate or standing instruction to invest in one or more SFC-authorised funds under specific circumstances, eg, using idle money in a client’s securities trading account with an aim to generate additional returns, albeit without any guaranteed or specific rates.
These SFC-authorised funds and services were often promoted by the distributors to the public through aggressive and high-profile marketing campaigns.
Guaranteed returns
Section 103 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO)

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

The SFC wishes to remind intermediaries who engage in promotional activities that these guaranteed return arrangements may constitute a "structured product" under the SFO if the return to investors is determined by reference to the change in value of any securities (including funds).

It is an offence under section 103 of the SFO for a person to issue an advertisement, invitation or document which is or contains an invitation to the Hong Kong public to enter into or offer to enter into any structured products, unless the SFC has authorised the issue or an exemption applies.

SFC-authorised funds without guaranteed features are required to highlight in their offering documents that they do not have these features and that investors may not get back the principal of their investment1. As such, any guaranteed returns provided by distributors may create a misleading impression that these returns are provided by the underlying fund(s).
Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct2

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client. The purpose of the requirement is to avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the features and risks of a particular product. If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

In light of the concerns set out from paragraphs 5 to 10 above, when offering or promoting funds, distributors should not offer additional returns (which are not part of the product features set out in the relevant offering documents) or other incentives to investors in breach of section 103 of the SFO or paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct.
Lock-up period and dealing frequency

When distributing SFC-authorised funds, some distributors imposed a lock-up period on their clients’ investments or lowered the funds’ dealing frequency. For instance, clients’ redemption was only allowed on a weekly or monthly basis even though the fund provided daily dealing arrangements.

Distributors should act fairly and in the best interests of their clients in providing services in accordance with General Principle 1 (Honesty and fairness) of the Code of Conduct. They should not restrict a client’s right to redeem his or her investment in a fund pursuant to the dealing frequency specified in the fund’s offering documents. Such restrictions would limit the client’s ability to make effective and timely investment decisions in response to changing market conditions or individual circumstances.

While distributors of SFC-authorised funds may have different fund dealing procedures or cut-off times for administrative efficiency, the SFC expects them to use their best endeavours to adhere to a fund’s dealing frequency as stipulated in its offering documents when dealing in the fund for clients, and not to reduce the fund’s dealing frequency.
Other marketing issues

In some cases, distributors offered or marketed the services described in paragraph 3 above without any guaranteed rates of return, but highlighted the regular interest payments or distribution features of the services prominently (eg, interest generated daily, or clients’ potential financial return from using such services), which would in fact be derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying fund(s). In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Where a distributor highlights in an advertisement the financial return of its services, which is in fact derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying SFC-authorised fund(s), the advertisement, particularly the presentation of financial return relating to the services, should be prepared in a manner that is consistent with the principles under the SFC’s Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes4.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.
Intermediaries Supervision Department                       Investment Products Division
Intermediaries Division                                                             Securities and Futures Commission
Securities and Futures Commission

1 Pursuant to 6.4 of the Overarching Principles Section as set out in the SFC Handbook for Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds, Investment-Linked Assurance Schemes and Unlisted Structured Investment Products, offering documents of an SFC-authorised fund shall contain the information necessary for investors to be able to make an informed judgement of the investment whilst all key features and risks of the fund shall be highlighted prominently in a succinct manner for investors.
2 The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (Code of Conduct).
3 The answer to question 1 of the frequently asked questions on the Code of Conduct issued by the SFC on 30 September 2010.
4 As supplemented by the frequently asked questions and other guidance issued by the SFC from time to time.

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one offered benefit in a distributor’s promotion of SFC-authorised funds.
A genuine discount can be treated as excepted even where it otherwise falls within the assessed gift category.
The unqualified words 'fees or charges' do not require those fees to relate to the promoted product.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction, with an unqualified fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it is a genuine discount of fees or charges. A true result identifies an offer caught by this selected restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: On this textual reading, a genuine discount on another service’s fees can fall within the exception even when used to promote a fund. This gives the unqualified exception broader reach than the product-related reading.

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one offered benefit in a distributor’s promotion of SFC-authorised funds.
A genuine discount can be treated as excepted even where it otherwise falls within the assessed gift category.
The surrounding product-promotion language implicitly confines the discount exception to fees or charges relating to that product; this qualification is not express.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction, with a product-related fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it is a genuine discount of fees or charges relating to the promoted product or product type. A true result identifies an offer caught by this selected restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: On this contextual reading, a discount on unrelated service fees remains caught if it qualifies as a gift linked to fund promotion. The anti-distraction purpose supports the narrower exception, but the absence of an express product-related qualifier is its strongest weakness.

assumptions.statement: Each evaluation concerns one identified benefit offer to one client; a campaign requires assessment of every relevant offer.
The actor must be a distributor as defined in u1; the Code's title alone does not expand this actor definition.
The general investment-product wording in u14 determines product scope.
Product-type linkage in the promotion is sufficient; proof of actual distraction is not an additional condition.
Unknown classification or scope facts remain unknown.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: general-product gift-offer restriction. For an intermediary distributing SFC-authorised funds, an identified benefit offered to a client in promoting a specific investment product or a particular product type is caught by the 'should not offer' restriction if it is a gift and is not a qualifying fee-or-charge discount. This includes promotional linkage to a fund type or fund house. The restriction does not depend on the arrangement being a structured product or on demonstrated distraction.
candidate.revision_reason: A defined distributor's non-discount gift promoting a specific investment product outside SFC-authorised funds can be caught. The strongest uncertainty is whether the circular's fund-specific setting limits the otherwise general product wording.
candidate.subject_unit: Whether an identified offer is caught by the selected paragraph-10 gift restriction

assumptions.statement: Each evaluation concerns one identified benefit offer to one client; a campaign requires assessment of every relevant offer.
The actor must be a distributor as defined in u1; the Code's title alone does not expand this actor definition.
The circular's SFC-authorised-fund context limits this selected application of the general wording quoted in u14.
Product-type linkage in the promotion is sufficient; proof of actual distraction is not an additional condition.
Unknown classification or scope facts remain unknown.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: fund-context gift-offer restriction. For an intermediary distributing SFC-authorised funds, an identified benefit offered to a client in promoting a specific SFC-authorised fund or a particular type of such funds is caught by the 'should not offer' restriction if it is a gift and is not a qualifying fee-or-charge discount. Product-type linkage includes relevant funds offered by certain fund houses. Structured-product status and actual distraction are not additional conditions.
candidate.revision_reason: The same distributor's gift promoting only a different investment product is outside this selected application, while gifts connected to SFC-authorised funds remain covered. Outside scope does not mean permitted under the full Code. The strongest uncertainty is that u14 itself states no express SFC-authorised-fund limitation.
candidate.subject_unit: Whether an identified offer is caught by the selected paragraph-10 gift restriction

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one identified promotional offer by an intermediary distributing SFC-authorised funds.
The result is a screen for the selected paragraph-10 gift-promotion control only, evaluated when scope is true.
Gift, discount and product-link classifications must be supplied from evidence and judgment; unknown classifications remain unknown.
No independent requirement to prove actual investor distraction is added: the text states distraction as the purpose and rationale.

candidate.controlled_language: For the selected paragraph-10 gift-promotion control, an in-scope distributor should not offer a gift in a client promotion connected to a specific investment product or particular product type unless the benefit qualifies as a discount of fees or charges. The linked-product-type explanation carries the same exception. Structured-product classification and section 103 authorisation are separate issues. The strongest unresolved issue is classification of borderline rebates and incentives, which the retained text and absent FAQ do not settle.
candidate.revision_reason: The supported reading attaches the exception to qualifying fee discounts and reaches both individual-product and product-type promotions. For a concrete classification boundary, consider a cash payment after subscribing to funds from one fund house, equal to the subscription fee. If it genuinely reduces that fee, the selected screen passes; if it is a separate gift merely measured by the fee, it fails. The supplied text does not decide which classification applies, so these are unresolved applications rather than two asserted legal rules. By contrast, excluding all fund-house-wide promotions because no single fund is named is contradicted by the express example.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction with an unqualified fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it genuinely discounts fees or charges, including fees for another service. A true result concerns this restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: Retains the parent’s stronger literal reading: a genuine discount on unrelated service fees is excepted from this selected restriction. In the supplied snapshot, scope is true but the result remains unknown because is_fee_discount is unknown. The DIFFERENT label cannot justify assigning that fact. The hypothesis that a discount exception also clears section 103 fails because u13 and u15 preserve separate controls.

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one offered benefit in a distributor’s promotion of SFC-authorised funds.
A genuine discount can be treated as excepted even where it otherwise falls within the assessed gift category.
The product-specific context and anti-distraction purpose imply that excepted fees or charges must relate to the promoted product or product type.
This implied limitation is a provisional purposive reading, not an express condition in the retained wording.
Unknown facts remain unknown; Boolean conclusions may nevertheless follow where a known fact makes an exception unavailable.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction with a product-related fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it genuinely discounts fees or charges relating to the promoted product or product type. A true result concerns this restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: Narrows the exception to reductions in costs relating to the promoted product. An unrelated-service discount can distract from that product’s risks like another promotional gift. In the supplied snapshot, scope and result are true because gift_offered is true and discount_relates_to_promoted_product is false, regardless of the unknown is_fee_discount. This distinguishes the rival from r1 without changing fact meanings. The strongest objection is that u14 never expressly says 'fees of the promoted product'; its purpose cannot conclusively supply those words.

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one offered benefit in a distributor’s promotion of SFC-authorised funds.
A genuine discount can be treated as excepted even where it otherwise falls within the assessed gift category.
Product-promotion linkage determines the scope of the restriction but does not add an unstated limitation to the fees eligible for discount.
Unknown classifications remain unknown; the result is evaluated only within the stated scope.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction with an unqualified fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it genuinely constitutes a discount of fees or charges. The fees need not themselves relate to the promoted product. A true result identifies conduct caught by this selected restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: This reading separates the promotional connection of the benefit from the subject matter of the discounted fees. A genuine discount of unrelated service fees is excepted even when offered to promote a fund. It has the stronger express wording because the parenthetical contains no product-related qualifier. Its strongest uncertainty is whether the missing Code or FAQ narrows what counts as an eligible discount. In the supplied snapshots, scope is true and gift_offered is true, but is_fee_discount remains unknown: this reading's result remains unknown. The parent reading yields true because discount_relates_to_promoted_product is false. This explains a possible difference without treating unknown as false or identifying undisclosed node formulas.

assumptions.statement: The assessment concerns one offered benefit in a distributor’s promotion of SFC-authorised funds.
A genuine discount can be treated as excepted even where it otherwise falls within the assessed gift category.
The surrounding product-promotion language implicitly confines the discount exception to fees or charges relating to that product; this qualification is not express.
Unknown classifications remain unknown; the result is evaluated only within the stated scope.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: paragraph-10 gift-promotion restriction with a product-related fee-discount exception. Within scope, an offered gift is caught unless it genuinely discounts fees or charges relating to the promoted product or product type. A true result identifies conduct caught by this selected restriction only.
candidate.revision_reason: This retains the parent's contextual alternative: an unrelated-service discount remains caught when it is a gift connected with fund promotion. The anti-distraction purpose supports considering such benefits, but does not expressly narrow the parenthetical exception; that is the strongest weakness. With the supplied known gift and promotion facts and false product-relatedness, the result is true regardless of the unknown discount classification. A decisive fully known separation would require a genuine discount of unrelated fees: r1 would return false and r2 true. That is a conditional comparison, not an invented finding. The hypotheses that every additional return is automatically a gift, or that only public, online or guaranteed-return promotions qualify, are not supported by u13–u15. Incomparable bindings do not rebut either interpretation; equivalence within an undisclosed domain does not resolve this textual issue.

assumptions.statement: Evaluation concerns one identified benefit offer to one client.
The distributor definition in u1 governs actor scope.
The fund-specific framing in u1, u13 and u15 limits this circular’s application of u14.
Gift classification precedes the discount exception; neither additional returns nor incentives are automatically gifts.
Unknown facts remain unknown. An out-of-scope offer is not thereby lawful under the Code or other controls.

candidate.controlled_language: Selected control: fund-context gift-offer restriction. For a defined distributor offering a benefit to a client in promoting SFC-authorised funds or a relevant fund type, the offer is caught when it is a gift other than a qualifying fee-or-charge discount. The restriction includes fund-house linkage and does not require actual distraction or structured-product status. Other-product offers fall outside this selected contextual control, subject to unresolved external Code requirements.
candidate.revision_reason: Adds only the fund-subject scope condition, preserving identical fact meanings and gift outcome. A hypothetical known distributor offering a known non-discount gift with product linkage outside SFC-authorised funds separates the readings: the broader reading catches it; this reading places it outside the selected control. This is a proposed discriminating case, not supplied evidence. The strongest uncertainty is u14’s express general investment-product wording.

The circular defines distributors through SFC-authorised funds; its opening observations about licensed corporations do not establish that registered intermediaries are excluded. readings.distinction: The supported reading attaches the exception to qualifying fee discounts and reaches both individual-product and product-type promotions. For a concrete classification boundary, consider a cash payment after subscribing to funds from one fund house, equal to the subscription fee. If it genuinely reduces that fee, the selected screen passes; if it is a separate gift merely measured by the fee, it fails. The supplied text does not decide which classification applies, so these are unresolved applications rather than two asserted legal rules. By contrast, excluding all fund-house-wide promotions because no single fund is named is contradicted by the express example.

dimensions.explanation: Both readings assess one benefit offered by an intermediary distributing SFC-authorised funds, connected to promotion of a specific product or product type, including funds of particular fund houses. Public advertising and structured-product status are not prerequisites for this selected control.

Gift classification and genuine fee-discount classification require judgment. Additional returns may be gifts but are not automatically gifts. Whether the discounted fees concern the promoted product is a separate fact, held stable across alternatives.

The parenthetical clearly excepts fee discounts from the gift restriction. Its unqualified wording supports discounts on any service, while the product-specific setting and anti-distraction purpose support a narrower, implied product-related limitation. The latter is less explicit. Section 103 authorisation or exemptions do not transfer to paragraph 3.11.

'May be considered a gift' preserves classification uncertainty; the separate marketing 'must' and dealing-frequency best-endeavours language do not alter it.

dimensions.explanation: Both readings concern one offered benefit in distribution of SFC-authorised funds. The actor is an intermediary distributing those funds. Product or product-type promotion includes linkage to funds of certain fund houses; online delivery, public advertising, a guarantee and demonstrated distraction are not express prerequisites. The broader reach of the underlying Code beyond this circular is unresolved.

Gift classification and genuine fee-discount classification require separate judgments. 'May be considered a gift' does not make all additional returns gifts. Actual fund return, distributor top-up and promoted service return are distinct. Neither 'gift' nor 'discount' receives an exhaustive definition here.

The express discount exception attaches to gifts. The rival question is whether product linkage limits only the promotion being assessed or also the fees eligible for discount. Section 103 authorisation/exemptions and dealing-procedure flexibility do not attach to this gift rule.

The selected rule says 'should not', described as a requirement. The Boolean result identifies conduct caught by that restriction; it does not establish a statutory offence or complete compliance. Possible gift classification and discretionary regulatory action remain distinct from the restriction itself.

30 September 2010 identifies issuance of the cited FAQ, not commencement of this circular or the selected restriction. No applicable assessment-period rule is supplied. The synthetic snapshot date supplies no legal effective date, and guidance issued 'from time to time' requires version identification.

units.text: This circular summarises the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) recent observations of licensed corporations’ practices in offering and promoting SFC-authorised funds. Intermediaries who distribute these funds (distributors) have been offering additional returns or other incentives that may divert the client’s focus from properly considering the risks and features of the underlying funds. This circular also highlights the legal and regulatory requirements to be met by distributors.
Background

In some cases, distributors promoted SFC-authorised funds (often via online platforms) and offered or imposed additional or distinct features or restrictions (eg, “guaranteed returns” or “lock-up periods”) beyond the product features set out in the funds’ offering documents.

In other cases, distributors asked clients to provide a mandate or standing instruction to invest in one or more SFC-authorised funds under specific circumstances, eg, using idle money in a client’s securities trading account with an aim to generate additional returns, albeit without any guaranteed or specific rates.
These SFC-authorised funds and services were often promoted by the distributors to the public through aggressive and high-profile marketing campaigns.
Guaranteed returns
Section 103 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO)

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

The SFC wishes to remind intermediaries who engage in promotional activities that these guaranteed return arrangements may constitute a "structured product" under the SFO if the return to investors is determined by reference to the change in value of any securities (including funds).

It is an offence under section 103 of the SFO for a person to issue an advertisement, invitation or document which is or contains an invitation to the Hong Kong public to enter into or offer to enter into any structured products, unless the SFC has authorised the issue or an exemption applies.

SFC-authorised funds without guaranteed features are required to highlight in their offering documents that they do not have these features and that investors may not get back the principal of their investment1. As such, any guaranteed returns provided by distributors may create a misleading impression that these returns are provided by the underlying fund(s).
Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct2

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client. The purpose of the requirement is to avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the features and risks of a particular product. If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

In light of the concerns set out from paragraphs 5 to 10 above, when offering or promoting funds, distributors should not offer additional returns (which are not part of the product features set out in the relevant offering documents) or other incentives to investors in breach of section 103 of the SFO or paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct.
Lock-up period and dealing frequency

When distributing SFC-authorised funds, some distributors imposed a lock-up period on their clients’ investments or lowered the funds’ dealing frequency. For instance, clients’ redemption was only allowed on a weekly or monthly basis even though the fund provided daily dealing arrangements.

Distributors should act fairly and in the best interests of their clients in providing services in accordance with General Principle 1 (Honesty and fairness) of the Code of Conduct. They should not restrict a client’s right to redeem his or her investment in a fund pursuant to the dealing frequency specified in the fund’s offering documents. Such restrictions would limit the client’s ability to make effective and timely investment decisions in response to changing market conditions or individual circumstances.

While distributors of SFC-authorised funds may have different fund dealing procedures or cut-off times for administrative efficiency, the SFC expects them to use their best endeavours to adhere to a fund’s dealing frequency as stipulated in its offering documents when dealing in the fund for clients, and not to reduce the fund’s dealing frequency.
Other marketing issues

In some cases, distributors offered or marketed the services described in paragraph 3 above without any guaranteed rates of return, but highlighted the regular interest payments or distribution features of the services prominently (eg, interest generated daily, or clients’ potential financial return from using such services), which would in fact be derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying fund(s). In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Where a distributor highlights in an advertisement the financial return of its services, which is in fact derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying SFC-authorised fund(s), the advertisement, particularly the presentation of financial return relating to the services, should be prepared in a manner that is consistent with the principles under the SFC’s Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes4.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.
Intermediaries Supervision Department                       Investment Products Division
Intermediaries Division                                                             Securities and Futures Commission
Securities and Futures Commission

1 Pursuant to 6.4 of the Overarching Principles Section as set out in the SFC Handbook for Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds, Investment-Linked Assurance Schemes and Unlisted Structured Investment Products, offering documents of an SFC-authorised fund shall contain the information necessary for investors to be able to make an informed judgement of the investment whilst all key features and risks of the fund shall be highlighted prominently in a succinct manner for investors.
2 The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (Code of Conduct).
3 The answer to question 1 of the frequently asked questions on the Code of Conduct issued by the SFC on 30 September 2010.
4 As supplemented by the frequently asked questions and other guidance issued by the SFC from time to time.

units.text: This circular summarises the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) recent observations of licensed corporations’ practices in offering and promoting SFC-authorised funds. Intermediaries who distribute these funds (distributors) have been offering additional returns or other incentives that may divert the client’s focus from properly considering the risks and features of the underlying funds. This circular also highlights the legal and regulatory requirements to be met by distributors.
Background

In some cases, distributors promoted SFC-authorised funds (often via online platforms) and offered or imposed additional or distinct features or restrictions (eg, “guaranteed returns” or “lock-up periods”) beyond the product features set out in the funds’ offering documents.

In other cases, distributors asked clients to provide a mandate or standing instruction to invest in one or more SFC-authorised funds under specific circumstances, eg, using idle money in a client’s securities trading account with an aim to generate additional returns, albeit without any guaranteed or specific rates.
These SFC-authorised funds and services were often promoted by the distributors to the public through aggressive and high-profile marketing campaigns.
Guaranteed returns
Section 103 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO)

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

The SFC wishes to remind intermediaries who engage in promotional activities that these guaranteed return arrangements may constitute a "structured product" under the SFO if the return to investors is determined by reference to the change in value of any securities (including funds).

It is an offence under section 103 of the SFO for a person to issue an advertisement, invitation or document which is or contains an invitation to the Hong Kong public to enter into or offer to enter into any structured products, unless the SFC has authorised the issue or an exemption applies.

SFC-authorised funds without guaranteed features are required to highlight in their offering documents that they do not have these features and that investors may not get back the principal of their investment1. As such, any guaranteed returns provided by distributors may create a misleading impression that these returns are provided by the underlying fund(s).
Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct2

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client. The purpose of the requirement is to avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the features and risks of a particular product. If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

In light of the concerns set out from paragraphs 5 to 10 above, when offering or promoting funds, distributors should not offer additional returns (which are not part of the product features set out in the relevant offering documents) or other incentives to investors in breach of section 103 of the SFO or paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct.
Lock-up period and dealing frequency

When distributing SFC-authorised funds, some distributors imposed a lock-up period on their clients’ investments or lowered the funds’ dealing frequency. For instance, clients’ redemption was only allowed on a weekly or monthly basis even though the fund provided daily dealing arrangements.

Distributors should act fairly and in the best interests of their clients in providing services in accordance with General Principle 1 (Honesty and fairness) of the Code of Conduct. They should not restrict a client’s right to redeem his or her investment in a fund pursuant to the dealing frequency specified in the fund’s offering documents. Such restrictions would limit the client’s ability to make effective and timely investment decisions in response to changing market conditions or individual circumstances.

While distributors of SFC-authorised funds may have different fund dealing procedures or cut-off times for administrative efficiency, the SFC expects them to use their best endeavours to adhere to a fund’s dealing frequency as stipulated in its offering documents when dealing in the fund for clients, and not to reduce the fund’s dealing frequency.
Other marketing issues

In some cases, distributors offered or marketed the services described in paragraph 3 above without any guaranteed rates of return, but highlighted the regular interest payments or distribution features of the services prominently (eg, interest generated daily, or clients’ potential financial return from using such services), which would in fact be derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying fund(s). In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Where a distributor highlights in an advertisement the financial return of its services, which is in fact derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying SFC-authorised fund(s), the advertisement, particularly the presentation of financial return relating to the services, should be prepared in a manner that is consistent with the principles under the SFC’s Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes4.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.
Intermediaries Supervision Department                       Investment Products Division
Intermediaries Division                                                             Securities and Futures Commission
Securities and Futures Commission

1 Pursuant to 6.4 of the Overarching Principles Section as set out in the SFC Handbook for Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds, Investment-Linked Assurance Schemes and Unlisted Structured Investment Products, offering documents of an SFC-authorised fund shall contain the information necessary for investors to be able to make an informed judgement of the investment whilst all key features and risks of the fund shall be highlighted prominently in a succinct manner for investors.
2 The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (Code of Conduct).
3 The answer to question 1 of the frequently asked questions on the Code of Conduct issued by the SFC on 30 September 2010.
4 As supplemented by the frequently asked questions and other guidance issued by the SFC from time to time.

units.text: This circular summarises the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) recent observations of licensed corporations’ practices in offering and promoting SFC-authorised funds. Intermediaries who distribute these funds (distributors) have been offering additional returns or other incentives that may divert the client’s focus from properly considering the risks and features of the underlying funds. This circular also highlights the legal and regulatory requirements to be met by distributors.
Background

In some cases, distributors promoted SFC-authorised funds (often via online platforms) and offered or imposed additional or distinct features or restrictions (eg, “guaranteed returns” or “lock-up periods”) beyond the product features set out in the funds’ offering documents.

In other cases, distributors asked clients to provide a mandate or standing instruction to invest in one or more SFC-authorised funds under specific circumstances, eg, using idle money in a client’s securities trading account with an aim to generate additional returns, albeit without any guaranteed or specific rates.
These SFC-authorised funds and services were often promoted by the distributors to the public through aggressive and high-profile marketing campaigns.
Guaranteed returns
Section 103 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO)

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

The SFC wishes to remind intermediaries who engage in promotional activities that these guaranteed return arrangements may constitute a "structured product" under the SFO if the return to investors is determined by reference to the change in value of any securities (including funds).

It is an offence under section 103 of the SFO for a person to issue an advertisement, invitation or document which is or contains an invitation to the Hong Kong public to enter into or offer to enter into any structured products, unless the SFC has authorised the issue or an exemption applies.

SFC-authorised funds without guaranteed features are required to highlight in their offering documents that they do not have these features and that investors may not get back the principal of their investment1. As such, any guaranteed returns provided by distributors may create a misleading impression that these returns are provided by the underlying fund(s).
Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct2

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client. The purpose of the requirement is to avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the features and risks of a particular product. If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

In light of the concerns set out from paragraphs 5 to 10 above, when offering or promoting funds, distributors should not offer additional returns (which are not part of the product features set out in the relevant offering documents) or other incentives to investors in breach of section 103 of the SFO or paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct.
Lock-up period and dealing frequency

When distributing SFC-authorised funds, some distributors imposed a lock-up period on their clients’ investments or lowered the funds’ dealing frequency. For instance, clients’ redemption was only allowed on a weekly or monthly basis even though the fund provided daily dealing arrangements.

Distributors should act fairly and in the best interests of their clients in providing services in accordance with General Principle 1 (Honesty and fairness) of the Code of Conduct. They should not restrict a client’s right to redeem his or her investment in a fund pursuant to the dealing frequency specified in the fund’s offering documents. Such restrictions would limit the client’s ability to make effective and timely investment decisions in response to changing market conditions or individual circumstances.

While distributors of SFC-authorised funds may have different fund dealing procedures or cut-off times for administrative efficiency, the SFC expects them to use their best endeavours to adhere to a fund’s dealing frequency as stipulated in its offering documents when dealing in the fund for clients, and not to reduce the fund’s dealing frequency.
Other marketing issues

In some cases, distributors offered or marketed the services described in paragraph 3 above without any guaranteed rates of return, but highlighted the regular interest payments or distribution features of the services prominently (eg, interest generated daily, or clients’ potential financial return from using such services), which would in fact be derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying fund(s). In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Where a distributor highlights in an advertisement the financial return of its services, which is in fact derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying SFC-authorised fund(s), the advertisement, particularly the presentation of financial return relating to the services, should be prepared in a manner that is consistent with the principles under the SFC’s Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes4.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.
Intermediaries Supervision Department                       Investment Products Division
Intermediaries Division                                                             Securities and Futures Commission
Securities and Futures Commission

1 Pursuant to 6.4 of the Overarching Principles Section as set out in the SFC Handbook for Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds, Investment-Linked Assurance Schemes and Unlisted Structured Investment Products, offering documents of an SFC-authorised fund shall contain the information necessary for investors to be able to make an informed judgement of the investment whilst all key features and risks of the fund shall be highlighted prominently in a succinct manner for investors.
2 The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (Code of Conduct).
3 The answer to question 1 of the frequently asked questions on the Code of Conduct issued by the SFC on 30 September 2010.
4 As supplemented by the frequently asked questions and other guidance issued by the SFC from time to time.

dimensions.explanation: The circular defines distributors by distribution of SFC-authorised funds, while u14 restates a control using general investment-product language. The alternatives differ over whether this selected control reaches those distributors' promotions of other investment products. Neither imports the separate section 103 Hong Kong-public condition.

Gift is not exhaustively defined. Additional returns and incentives may qualify, rather than necessarily qualifying. Product types expressly include certain fund types and funds from certain fund houses. Whether a benefit is a genuine fee discount and whether it has the required promotional connection require judgment.

The fee-or-charge discount parenthesis qualifies gifts under the selected restriction, including gifts linked to a product type. It does not exempt conduct from other provisions. No actual-distraction test or structured-product exemption is stated for this control. The text does not settle which fees qualify or the treatment of mixed benefits.

The selected wording is 'should not', reinforced by 'requirement' and 'will be bound'. It supports a normative restriction, without establishing that every breach is a statutory offence. 'May be considered a gift' leaves classification contingent. The formalized outcome identifies an offer caught by this restriction, not liability or overall compliance.

The restriction concerns offering gifts in promotion, without a supplied commencement date, deadline or transitional rule. The FAQ date, 2010-09-30, identifies a referenced document and is not established as the control's effective date. Later advertising guidance does not supply that date.

Paragraph 3.11 and FAQ question 1 are material unprovided authorities. The packet's external-authorities.23ec46 dependency has no source hash. Statutory, Handbook and advertising provisions remain separate contextual dependencies; their full content or current versions cannot be inferred from the extracts.

readings.distinction: The supported reading attaches the exception to qualifying fee discounts and reaches both individual-product and product-type promotions. For a concrete classification boundary, consider a cash payment after subscribing to funds from one fund house, equal to the subscription fee. If it genuinely reduces that fee, the selected screen passes; if it is a separate gift merely measured by the fee, it fails. The supplied text does not decide which classification applies, so these are unresolved applications rather than two asserted legal rules. By contrast, excluding all fund-house-wide promotions because no single fund is named is contradicted by the express example.

dimensions.explanation: Both readings assess one benefit offered by an intermediary distributing SFC-authorised funds, connected to promotion of a specific product or product type, including funds of particular fund houses. Public advertising and structured-product status are not prerequisites for this selected control.

Gift classification and genuine fee-discount classification require judgment. Additional returns may be gifts but are not automatically gifts. Whether the discounted fees concern the promoted product is a separate fact, held stable across alternatives.

The parenthetical clearly excepts fee discounts from the gift restriction. Its unqualified wording supports discounts on any service, while the product-specific setting and anti-distraction purpose support a narrower, implied product-related limitation. The latter is less explicit. Section 103 authorisation or exemptions do not transfer to paragraph 3.11.

The selected control retains 'should not' as a regulatory restriction. A true result identifies an offer caught by that restriction, not a criminal offence or overall noncompliance. 'May be considered a gift' preserves classification uncertainty; the separate marketing 'must' and dealing-frequency best-endeavours language do not alter it.

30 September 2010 dates the cited FAQ, not commencement of this circular or the gift restriction. No operative date or applicable version is supplied. The synthetic snapshot date supplies no legal commencement evidence; future guidance is expressly contemplated.

external-authorities.23ec46 is missing. The full paragraph 3.11 and FAQ answer are needed to resolve exception breadth and classification. The SFO, Handbook, paragraph 2.3 and Advertising Guidelines are separate dependencies, not grounds for expanding this selected control.

dimensions.explanation: Both readings concern one offered benefit in distribution of SFC-authorised funds. The actor is an intermediary distributing those funds. Product or product-type promotion includes linkage to funds of certain fund houses; online delivery, public advertising, a guarantee and demonstrated distraction are not express prerequisites. The broader reach of the underlying Code beyond this circular is unresolved.

Gift classification and genuine fee-discount classification require separate judgments. 'May be considered a gift' does not make all additional returns gifts. Actual fund return, distributor top-up and promoted service return are distinct. Neither 'gift' nor 'discount' receives an exhaustive definition here.

The express discount exception attaches to gifts. The rival question is whether product linkage limits only the promotion being assessed or also the fees eligible for discount. Section 103 authorisation/exemptions and dealing-procedure flexibility do not attach to this gift rule.

The selected rule says 'should not', described as a requirement. The Boolean result identifies conduct caught by that restriction; it does not establish a statutory offence or complete compliance. Possible gift classification and discretionary regulatory action remain distinct from the restriction itself.

30 September 2010 identifies issuance of the cited FAQ, not commencement of this circular or the selected restriction. No applicable assessment-period rule is supplied. The synthetic snapshot date supplies no legal effective date, and guidance issued 'from time to time' requires version identification.

external-authorities.23ec46 is missing. The full Code paragraph 3.11 and FAQ answer could resolve classification, scope and exception breadth. Section 103, disclosure principles and advertising guidance are separate dependencies; the retained summary cannot establish their complete conditions.

questions: Does the applicable full text of paragraph 3.11 or FAQ question 1 expressly limit the discount exception to fees relating to the promoted product?
What criteria distinguish a genuine fee discount from a cash gift or distributor-funded top-up, particularly for account-wide rebates?
Which versions of the Code and FAQ apply at the assessment date, and when did the relevant provisions take effect?
What formulas and fact bindings underlie the diagnostic node pairs? Their status labels alone cannot establish the substantive cause of disagreement or equivalence.

readings.distinction: This retains the parent's contextual alternative: an unrelated-service discount remains caught when it is a gift connected with fund promotion. The anti-distraction purpose supports considering such benefits, but does not expressly narrow the parenthetical exception; that is the strongest weakness. A decisive fully known separation would require a genuine discount of unrelated fees: r1 would return false and r2 true. That is a conditional comparison, not an invented finding. dimensions.explanation: The selected control addresses distributors promoting a specific investment product or particular product type to a client. The circular defines distributors through SFC-authorised funds; its opening observations about licensed corporations do not establish that registered intermediaries are excluded. The full Code’s application beyond this circular remains unresolved.

Neither gift nor discount of fees or charges is exhaustively defined. Guaranteed returns and other incentives may be gifts; classification is not automatic. Fund types and funds from particular fund houses expressly illustrate product-type links.

The fee-discount parenthesis qualifies the gifts covered by paragraph 3.11, including the later linked-gift explanation. Section 103 authorisation or exemption is a separate exception and does not excuse a gift under paragraph 3.11.

The control concerns offering gifts in promotion, without requiring payment or completed investment. No commencement date, transition rule, or assessment date is supplied. The date 2010-09-30 identifies the referenced FAQ’s issue date, not this control’s commencement.

readings.distinction: The supported reading attaches the exception to qualifying fee discounts and reaches both individual-product and product-type promotions. For a concrete classification boundary, consider a cash payment after subscribing to funds from one fund house, equal to the subscription fee. If it genuinely reduces that fee, the selected screen passes; if it is a separate gift merely measured by the fee, it fails. The supplied text does not decide which classification applies, so these are unresolved applications rather than two asserted legal rules. By contrast, excluding all fund-house-wide promotions because no single fund is named is contradicted by the express example.

dimensions.explanation: The selected control addresses distributors promoting a specific investment product or particular product type to a client. The circular concerns SFC-authorised funds; its opening reference to licensed corporations does not conclusively exclude registered intermediaries. Public advertising, online distribution and guaranteed returns are not necessary triggers.

Distributors are identified as intermediaries distributing these funds. Gift and discount are not exhaustively defined. Additional returns or incentives may qualify as gifts, rather than necessarily doing so. Product types expressly include certain fund types and funds from certain fund houses.

The discount parenthesis qualifies gifts under the selected control, including gifts linked to a product type. Whether eligible fees must relate to that promoted product is unresolved. Section 103 authorisation or exemption is not stated to excuse the gift restriction.

The source states that distributors 'should not' offer gifts and calls this a requirement. The formalizations identify offers caught by that stated restriction; they do not determine a criminal offence, sanction, or overall compliance. 'May be considered a gift' leaves classification unresolved.

No circular commencement date or transition period is supplied. The 30 September 2010 date identifies the referenced FAQ’s issuance, not the selected control’s effective date. Applicable versions cannot be determined from the packet.

Paragraph 3.11 and FAQ question 1 are the principal unresolved authorities. Section 103 is a separate dependency; the Handbook, paragraph 2.3 and advertising guidance concern surrounding controls. The external-authorities dependency has no supplied text or hash, so no additional content is inferred.

If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement
as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

reading.statement: Selected control: fund-context gift-offer restriction. For a defined distributor offering a benefit to a client in promoting SFC-authorised funds or a relevant fund type, the offer is caught when it is a gift other than a qualifying fee-or-charge discount. The restriction includes fund-house linkage and does not require actual distraction or structured-product status. Other-product offers fall outside this selected contextual control, subject to unresolved external Code requirements.

retained_uncited_units.text: Background

In some cases, distributors promoted SFC-authorised funds (often via online platforms) and offered or imposed additional or distinct features or restrictions (eg, “guaranteed returns” or “lock-up periods”) beyond the product features set out in the funds’ offering documents.

In other cases, distributors asked clients to provide a mandate or standing instruction to invest in one or more SFC-authorised funds under specific circumstances, eg, using idle money in a client’s securities trading account with an aim to generate additional returns, albeit without any guaranteed or specific rates.
These SFC-authorised funds and services were often promoted by the distributors to the public through aggressive and high-profile marketing campaigns.
Guaranteed returns
Section 103 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO)

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

The SFC wishes to remind intermediaries who engage in promotional activities that these guaranteed return arrangements may constitute a "structured product" under the SFO if the return to investors is determined by reference to the change in value of any securities (including funds).

It is an offence under section 103 of the SFO for a person to issue an advertisement, invitation or document which is or contains an invitation to the Hong Kong public to enter into or offer to enter into any structured products, unless the SFC has authorised the issue or an exemption applies.

SFC-authorised funds without guaranteed features are required to highlight in their offering documents that they do not have these features and that investors may not get back the principal of their investment1. As such, any guaranteed returns provided by distributors may create a misleading impression that these returns are provided by the underlying fund(s).
Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct2

In light of the concerns set out from paragraphs 5 to 10 above, when offering or promoting funds, distributors should not offer additional returns (which are not part of the product features set out in the relevant offering documents) or other incentives to investors in breach of section 103 of the SFO or paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct.
Lock-up period and dealing frequency

When distributing SFC-authorised funds, some distributors imposed a lock-up period on their clients’ investments or lowered the funds’ dealing frequency. For instance, clients’ redemption was only allowed on a weekly or monthly basis even though the fund provided daily dealing arrangements.

Distributors should act fairly and in the best interests of their clients in providing services in accordance with General Principle 1 (Honesty and fairness) of the Code of Conduct. They should not restrict a client’s right to redeem his or her investment in a fund pursuant to the dealing frequency specified in the fund’s offering documents. Such restrictions would limit the client’s ability to make effective and timely investment decisions in response to changing market conditions or individual circumstances.

While distributors of SFC-authorised funds may have different fund dealing procedures or cut-off times for administrative efficiency, the SFC expects them to use their best endeavours to adhere to a fund’s dealing frequency as stipulated in its offering documents when dealing in the fund for clients, and not to reduce the fund’s dealing frequency.
Other marketing issues

In some cases, distributors offered or marketed the services described in paragraph 3 above without any guaranteed rates of return, but highlighted the regular interest payments or distribution features of the services prominently (eg, interest generated daily, or clients’ potential financial return from using such services), which would in fact be derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying fund(s). In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Where a distributor highlights in an advertisement the financial return of its services, which is in fact derived from the actual return(s) of the underlying SFC-authorised fund(s), the advertisement, particularly the presentation of financial return relating to the services, should be prepared in a manner that is consistent with the principles under the SFC’s Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes4.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.
Intermediaries Supervision Department                       Investment Products Division
Intermediaries Division                                                             Securities and Futures Commission
Securities and Futures Commission

2 The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (Code of Conduct).
3 The answer to question 1 of the frequently asked questions on the Code of Conduct issued by the SFC on 30 September 2010.
4 As supplemented by the frequently asked questions and other guidance issued by the SFC from time to time.

This circular summarises the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) recent observations of licensed corporations’ practices in offering and promoting SFC-authorised funds. In preparing invitations and advertisements to promote their services, intermediaries should ensure that they do not contain any misleading or deceptive information, and they must comply with paragraph 2.3 of the Code of Conduct.

Specifically, the advertisements of these services should avoid giving a misleading impression that the relevant services or underlying fund(s) would generate positive or guaranteed returns without any risk of loss. In addition, the advertisements should not draw a parallel between the services and the placement of cash on deposits, imply they are deposit-like arrangements (including any comparisons between the financial returns of the services and bank deposit rates), or suggest that the services are, or are equivalent to, bank deposits or savings (eg, by emphasising the services can address investors’ “savings needs”).
The SFC will closely monitor market practices concerning the promotion of SFC-authorised funds and may take regulatory action and issue further guidance where appropriate.

(declare-fun is_distributor.false () Bool)
(declare-fun is_distributor.true () Bool)
(declare-fun has_product_promotion_connection.false () Bool)
(declare-fun has_product_promotion_connection.true () Bool)
(declare-fun gift_offered.false () Bool)
(declare-fun gift_offered.true () Bool)
(declare-fun is_fee_discount.false () Bool)
(declare-fun is_fee_discount.true () Bool)
(declare-fun discount_relates_to_promoted_product.false () Bool)
(declare-fun discount_relates_to_promoted_product.true () Bool)
(assert (or (and is_distributor.true (not is_distributor.false))
    (and is_distributor.false (not is_distributor.true))
    (and (not is_distributor.true) (not is_distributor.false))))
(assert (or (and has_product_promotion_connection.true
         (not has_product_promotion_connection.false))
    (and has_product_promotion_connection.false
         (not has_product_promotion_connection.true))
    (and (not has_product_promotion_connection.true)
         (not has_product_promotion_connection.false))))
(assert (or (and gift_offered.true (not gift_offered.false))
    (and gift_offered.false (not gift_offered.true))
    (and (not gift_offered.true) (not gift_offered.false))))
(assert (or (and is_fee_discount.true (not is_fee_discount.false))
    (and is_fee_discount.false (not is_fee_discount.true))
    (and (not is_fee_discount.true) (not is_fee_discount.false))))
(assert (or (and discount_relates_to_promoted_product.true
         (not discount_relates_to_promoted_product.false))
    (and discount_relates_to_promoted_product.false
         (not discount_relates_to_promoted_product.true))
    (and (not discount_relates_to_promoted_product.true)
         (not discount_relates_to_promoted_product.false))))
(assert (let ((a!1 (ite (not (and is_distributor.true
                          has_product_promotion_connection.true))
                0
                (ite (and gift_offered.true is_fee_discount.false)
                     1
                     (ite (or gift_offered.false is_fee_discount.true) 2 0)))))
(let ((a!2 (and (= (ite (or is_distributor.false
                            has_product_promotion_connection.false)
                        4
                        a!1)
                   3)
                (= (ite (or is_distributor.false
                            has_product_promotion_connection.false)
                        4
                        a!1)
                   3)
                (distinct 0 0))))
  (or (distinct (ite (or is_distributor.false
                         has_product_promotion_connection.false)
                     4
                     a!1)
                (ite (or is_distributor.false
                         has_product_promotion_connection.false)
                     4
                     a!1))
      a!2))))

(model-add is_distributor.false () Bool true)
